record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Falconer for a forwarded reference and says he has begun arranging pigeon skeletons for comparison, may consult Falconer, and is preparing an abstract on species and varieties (P1–2). This is a Darwin-originated request/continuation; the forwarded note and any answer are not preserved here, so the pigeon work cannot identify a prompt.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin thanks Eyton, asks to borrow selected skeletons, offers his four-or-five-page pigeon notes for Eyton's criticism, and asks for a lesson from Falconer first (P1–5). His later questions concern dun horses and double shoulder stripes (P6–7). These are separate requests in one outgoing letter; no preserved Eyton prompt is identified.

record_reviews.summary: Darwin asks Eyton to observe whether mud clings to partridge, pheasant, or wader feet and, if possible, send dirt-clogged feet so Darwin can test for live seeds (P1–2). The request is explicitly about plant-seed distribution; the matching Eyton reply is 2343, but it reports little mud and does not establish a prior Darwin response to an Eyton letter.

record_reviews.summary: Eyton reports that he examined many partridge feet but found only slight dirt and no useful quantity, promising to send material if he obtains it (P1). The October 16 dateline and signature are Eyton's; this is a substantive reverse response to Darwin's 2338 request, with no evidence that it answers any other Darwin passage.

record_reviews.summary: Falconer dates the main letter October 25 and describes 800 deer antlers from a Welsh cave, with continuous variation that would look species-like in isolated specimens, then proposes studying change from glacial to modern reindeer (P1–5). A separately dated November 12 postscript says Darwin's note arrived the previous day and Falconer sent for the Origin copy, while completing the address and announcing his move to Torquay (P6–10). The scientific proposal and book-receipt postscript must remain separate.

record_reviews.summary: Owen says he will welcome Darwin's work and states that he already favours existing causes in the 'ordained becoming and incoming' of species (P1). He explains that philosophers rebuked his published position and that he tests species-making explanations against observed effects (P2), then credits Darwin's gifts (P3). This is Owen's response/position statement, but the preceding Darwin source is not preserved in this packet and the shared evolutionary topic is insufficient to identify one.
